title: Feel Like Yourself Again
body_text:
I found my mother's medication list folded inside a Bible in her nightstand the day after we buried her.

It was on a piece of yellow legal pad paper, the kind she used for grocery lists, in her tight little handwriting. 14 medications. Doses next to each one. Times of day in the margins. The names of three different cardiologists at the top.

She'd been carrying that list in her purse for the last 8 years of her life and I never knew.

I sat down on her side of the bed and read it twice. And then I read it a third time. And then I went to her kitchen drawer, the one to the left of the sink where she kept her reading glasses, and I started counting.

14 pairs of cheap reading glasses. The kind from the spinning rack at Walgreens. Black ones, tortoise shell ones, a pair with rhinestones on the temples that I'd never seen her wear.

Three pill organizers. One for the week. One for the month. A small one for travel.

A blood pressure cuff with the velcro worn soft.

A bottle of children's aspirin she'd been chewing one of every morning for as long as I could remember.

And my mother, Janelle Adeyemi Carter, had died at 67 of a stroke in the breakfast nook of her own kitchen on a Tuesday morning in February.

My name is Tamika. I'm 56 years old. I live in a small ranch house off Old Shell Road in Mobile, Alabama, about 12 minutes from the house my mother lived in for 38 years.

I'm a probate paralegal. I have been one for 28 years. I know how to clean out a dead person's house. I've helped clients do it dozens of times. I knew exactly what boxes to bring. I knew which days the Salvation Army would pick up furniture. I knew to bring a Sharpie and label everything for my sisters.

What I didn't know was that I would find her medication list in a Bible and have to sit down on the edge of her bed and cry like a child.

My mother was not a sick woman. That's the part that I want you to understand before I tell you the rest of this.

She walked 2 miles a day around the loop at Langan Park. She made her own collard greens and she didn't put a hambone in them anymore because her doctor told her to cut back on sodium. She went to Sunday service at Stewart Memorial AME. She volunteered Tuesdays at the community library shelving children's books.

She drank her coffee black. She didn't smoke. She had two glasses of red wine on Saturday nights and that was it.

She was on 14 medications anyway.

Three for blood pressure. Two for cholesterol. One for her thyroid. A blood thinner. A water pill. Something for her kidneys because of the water pill. Something for her stomach because of all the other pills. A statin. A second statin when the first one stopped working. And three I had to Google because I'd never even heard of them.

This is the part nobody warns you about. Your mother starts taking one pill in her 50s for blood pressure that was "just a little high." By her 60s she's on five. By her late 60s she's on 14 and her cardiologist is talking about adding a 15th.

And the whole time she's walking 2 miles a day and skipping the hambone and saying, baby, this is just what people my age have to do.

I rode in the front seat of her Buick to her appointments for the last 3 years of her life. I sat in those waiting rooms with the Keurig machine and the year old issues of Coastal Living and I watched my mother nod at every new prescription like she was being handed homework.

She'd come out, look at me, and shrug. She'd say, Tamika, what am I supposed to do. He's the doctor.

In January, exactly one month before she died, her cardiologist told her her LDL was up again. He said they needed to "explore other options." He used those words. Explore other options. As if a 67 year old woman who was already on two cholesterol medications was supposed to have a hearty appetite for exploration.

She had a stroke on February 11. In her breakfast nook. Holding a coffee cup. My father heard the cup hit the floor from the bathroom.

She was gone before the ambulance got to Springhill Memorial.

3 weeks after the funeral I went to my own primary care doctor for my annual.

I'd been putting it off for 14 months. I knew it. She knew it. My husband Derrick knew it.

I'm 56. I work at a desk all day. I do not walk 2 miles around Langan Park. I eat too much takeout from the Vietnamese place on Airport Boulevard because Derrick works late at his shop and I don't feel like cooking for one.

I sat in the chair across from Dr. Henley and she pulled up my numbers and her face did the thing. The thing where she's about to tell you something but she's pretending she isn't.

She said, Tamika, your LDL is 187.

She said, your blood pressure is 142 over 91.

She said, your A1C is creeping into a place we need to watch.

I started laughing. I actually laughed in her face. Not because it was funny. Because I had buried my mother 3 weeks earlier with 14 pills in her purse and now I was sitting in a doctor's office about to be handed my first prescription.

I said, Dr. Henley, my mother just died.

She said, I know.

I said, my mother was on 14 medications and walked 2 miles a day and died at 67.

She said, I know.

I said, I am not doing that. I am not doing what she did.

Dr. Henley is a good woman. She's about my age. She has a daughter at Auburn. She put her pen down and she looked at me and she said, Tamika, I hear you. But these numbers are real. Let's start with a low dose statin and we'll talk about the rest.

She wrote me a prescription. I took it.

I never filled it.

I drove home from that appointment and I sat in my car in my driveway for an hour and 20 minutes. The car was off. The sun was going down. Derrick's truck wasn't home yet.

And I made a promise out loud to my mama that I was not going to walk her road.

I started reading that night.

I'm a paralegal. Reading is what I do. I read contracts and probate filings and case law for a living, and I am very good at telling the difference between a source that knows what it's talking about and a source that's selling me something.

I read for 3 weeks. I read at night after Derrick went to bed. I read on my lunch break in the car. I read studies and forum threads and the boring medical literature that most people don't bother with.

I learned a few things I want to share with you because I wish someone had told my mother.

What I learned was that the way your body manages cholesterol and the way your body manages blood pressure are not 14 separate problems with 14 separate solutions. They're one problem with one root.

The arteries in your body have a thin inner lining. Smooth, slippery, alive. When that lining is healthy, blood flows clean. Cholesterol moves through without sticking. Pressure stays steady because the vessels stay flexible.

But there's a process happening inside every adult body where that lining gets irritated. Slowly. Decade by decade. By the time you're in your 50s and 60s, the irritation has been building for 30, 40 years. The lining stiffens. The body responds the only way it knows how, by sending repair cells to patch things up. Those patches are what eventually become the plaque your doctor measures with a number.

The cholesterol number itself isn't the disease. It's the smoke. The fire is the irritation in the lining.

Statins work on the smoke. They lower the number. They don't do much about the fire.

That's why my mother could be on two cholesterol medications and still have her LDL "creeping up" 8 years into treatment. The medicines were chasing the number. The fire was still burning.

I read about a lot of things in those 3 weeks. Omega 3s. Fiber. Beet root. Hawthorn. Magnesium. CoQ10. All things I'd heard of. All things that have something behind them but nothing that landed like a real answer.

And then on a Saturday morning in late March, sitting at my kitchen table with my second cup of coffee, I came across a research summary about a small green fruit I'd never heard of.

Amla.

The Indian gooseberry. Grown on trees on family farms across India and Nepal. It has been used in Ayurvedic medicine for something like 3,000 years.

It is one of the most concentrated natural sources of a particular kind of vitamin C in the world. But more than that, it carries a family of plant compounds called polyphenols that have been studied for their role in supporting healthy vascular function. The lining of the arteries. The very thing I'd been reading about.

The way the research framed it stopped me cold.

Amla works on the fire, not the smoke.

It supports the arterial lining. It supports the body's own regulation of cholesterol synthesis in the liver. It supports the smooth muscle in the vessel walls that keeps blood pressure flexible instead of stiff.

It's not a drug. It's not pretending to be one. It doesn't override the body. It supports what the body is already trying to do.

I sat in my kitchen and I cried for the second time in a month. Because what if my mother had known. What if somebody had told her in 1998 when she got that first prescription that there was a 3,000 year old fruit on the other side of the world that worked on the cause and not the symptom.

She would have eaten it for breakfast every day for the rest of her life.

I went down the rabbit hole all the way that weekend.

I found a company in Texas called Alevia. They make a pure amla extract in a capsule. No fillers. No fluff. They source the fruit from family farms in India, they test it independently in the United States, and they put it in a clean capsule with nothing else added.

They had a 90 day money back guarantee.

I'll tell you the truth because lying to you wouldn't help either of us. I have been burned before. I bought my mother a turmeric supplement from a TV ad in 2019 that did nothing. I bought her fish oil pills the size of my pinky that she gagged on every morning for 2 months. I bought myself an ashwagandha capsule from the vitamin store at Bel Air Mall that gave me a rash on my chest.

But this was different. The mechanism made sense. The science was thirty years old, not thirty days. And the guarantee meant if it didn't do anything I wasn't out anything but a few weeks of patience.

I ordered a bottle on a Sunday night. It came on Wednesday. I started taking one every morning with my coffee, sitting at the same table where I'd read about it.

The first 2 weeks I felt nothing.

I almost stopped at day 11. I called my sister Renee in Atlanta and told her about it and she said, baby, give it the full time. Mama always said you don't pull up a plant after 2 weeks to see if the roots are growing.

I kept taking it.

Week 3, I noticed I was sleeping through the night. I hadn't slept through the night in maybe 6 years. I'd been waking up at 3:14 in the morning like clockwork to use the bathroom and then lying there for an hour. I just stopped doing that.

Week 4, my rings fit different. I'd been taking my wedding band off at night for 3 years because my fingers swelled. I forgot to take it off one Tuesday and woke up and it was fine.

Week 6, I walked the dog around the block and I didn't have to stop at the corner to catch my breath. I'd been stopping at the corner for so long it had become a habit. I just walked past it.

Week 9, I went back to Dr. Henley. I told her I hadn't filled the statin. She started to fuss. Then she pulled up my labs.

My LDL had dropped 31 points.

My blood pressure was 124 over 79.

My A1C was back in the normal range.

She sat there with her glasses on the end of her nose and she said, Tamika, what did you do.

I told her. I told her exactly what I'd been doing. I told her about Alevia Amla. I told her about the reading. I told her about my mother's medication list in the Bible.

She didn't argue with me. She didn't push the statin. She closed my chart and she said, keep doing what you're doing. We'll check again in 3 months.

That was 7 months ago.

I'm not going to lie to you and tell you I'm a different woman. I'm still 56. I still work at a desk. I still eat too much pho on Tuesday nights when Derrick is at the shop.

But I'm not on a single prescription. I take one capsule of Alevia Amla every morning with my coffee. I take a fish oil at night. That's it. That's my whole list.

I went to my mother's grave on what would have been her 68th birthday. I sat there on the grass with a coffee from the McDonald's drive thru and I told her everything I'd learned. I told her about the fire and the smoke. I told her I was sorry I didn't know in time. I told her I was going to make sure my sisters knew. I told her I was going to make sure my daughter Jasmine, who is 31 and already has higher blood pressure than I want her to have, knew too.

I sat there for an hour and I talked to my mama like she was on the other side of the kitchen table.

I'm telling you all of this because if you're a Black woman in your 50s or 60s, if you watched your mother or your grandmother or your auntie disappear into a medication list, if you've been told that the road you're on is just what happens to women like us, please hear me.

That is not the only road. There is another one. I am walking it.

If you want to look at it for yourself, the company is Alevia. The product is Alevia Amla. They sell it from their own website and they have that 90 day money back guarantee, which is the only reason I had the courage to start. If it hadn't done anything for me I would have sent it back and gone back to square one. I called their customer line one time with a shipping question and the woman who answered was a real person in Texas who didn't rush me off the phone.

I take it every morning. My sister Renee takes it now. My cousin Doreen in Birmingham takes it. My daughter Jasmine started taking it last month.

Four generations of women in my family have been buried with their pill bottles. I am breaking the chain.

If you're sitting in a doctor's office and they're handing you your first prescription and something in your chest is telling you "wait," please listen to that voice. Listen to it before it gets quieter.

90 days. If it doesn't do anything, they send your money back. That's the whole deal.

👉 alevia.com/amla/33

P.S. I want to say this clearly. I'm not telling you to stop your medications. If you're on something, talk to your doctor. I never started mine in the first place, so I had nothing to come off of. But the women I know who have made changes did it with their doctor's involvement, slowly, over months, with their labs checked. Be smart. Be patient. Don't be reckless on my account.

P.P.S. My mother's medication list is folded in the front of my own Bible now. I keep it there to remind me what I'm walking away from. Every morning when I take my one capsule with my coffee I think about her. I think about the 14 pairs of reading glasses. I think about the way the cardiologist used the word "explore" like he was inviting her on a vacation. She deserved better. So do you.

P.P.P.S. If you have a daughter, please give her a bottle too. Don't wait until she's where I was. Whatever is happening in our blood, in our vessels, in our arteries, it didn't start at 56. It started at 26. The earlier she supports it the easier it stays supported. I wish my mother had known to give one to me when I was Jasmine's age. She didn't know. Now you do.

title: 👆  Read this if the allergies won’t go away
body_text:
Please STOP buying allergy meds for your dog.

I know that sounds insane when you're watching him chew through his own skin at 2am., but hear me out.

Because I'm about to tell you the one thing I figured out about dog allergies that I wish someone had told me 2 years and $3400 dollars ago.

It's the thing that explains why every drug stops working after three weeks. Why every supplement you've tried did nothing. Why your vet keeps adding more medications and your dog is still scratching.

I'm a dog groomer. Sixteen years in this industry. I didn't know it either.

And once you know it, the entire pet allergy industry stops making sense.

His name is Henry. Six year old Cavalier King Charles. My soul pup.

He started itching at two. Just seasonal. By year four it was year-round. By year five he was in the cone permanently. By year six the only thing my husband and I talked about over coffee in the morning was whether Henry made it through the night without tearing himself open.

In twelve months I spent $3400 dollars on him.

I'm going to tell you what that bought me.

NOTHING

Apoquel was first. $156 a month. Worked for three weeks then quit. Vet said increase the dose. I did. It quit again two weeks later.

Then Cytopoint shots. $189 every two weeks. Worked three weeks at a time. By month six we were going in early because the itching was coming back early.

Then Cyclosporine. Until his gums grew over his teeth so thick he couldn't chew kibble.

Then Zenrelia. Worked for fourteen days. Then he was scratching again.

By the fourth drug I knew something was wrong. Not with Henry. With the whole approach.

I just didn't know what yet.

Meanwhile I was running every grooming protocol I knew. Twice weekly chlorhexidine baths. Daily ear cleaning. Paw wipes. Oatmeal soaks. Coconut oil. Apple cider vinegar in his water bowl. Eight different supplements stacked in the cabinet above his food.

The cone wore the fur off the back of his neck.

He chewed his belly through the cone anyway.

One night I sat on the bathroom floor at 2am watching him scrape his face on the bath mat. Something broke. Not loud. Not crying. Just empty.

I grabbed my laptop and started typing things I'd never typed before.

"Why does Apoquel stop working."

"Dog still itching on Cytopoint."

Thousands of dog parents asking the same questions. Same story repeating in the answers: works for a few weeks, stops, vet adds something else, that stops too, dog still scratching.

Then I found one thread that wasn't like the others. Where everyone else was venting, one vet had actually answered.

What she wrote changed everything for me. I screenshotted it and read it back to myself five times.

"Allergies compromise the skin barrier, and then the microbes get in and set up infection. If you don't address the underlying cause AND the secondary infection, the allergy meds will not work."

The skin barrier.

Sixteen years grooming and I'd never heard those two words used together. Not from my vet. Not from the dermatologist. Not from any product I'd ever sold in my own salon.

So I went down the rabbit hole. And what I found explained every single failure of every single thing I'd tried.

Dogs have a layer in their skin made mostly of collagen. It's a wall. When the wall is intact, allergens stay on the outside where they belong.

When the wall breaks down, and it does, especially in dogs over two, gaps form. Pollen slips through. Dust mites burrow in. Grass proteins trigger massive immune responses. The immune system sees invaders and goes into overdrive.

That's the chronic itching. The mutilation. The hot spots. The 2am collar jingling.

And here's where I got angry.

Apoquel suppresses the immune response. Cytopoint blocks the itch signal. Cyclosporine and Zenrelia shut down the immune system more aggressively.

But none of them rebuild the wall.

It's like turning off the smoke alarm while the fire keeps burning. That's why every drug works for three weeks. That's why every drug stops. That's why your vet keeps adding more. The fire is still burning. The wall is still broken. The allergens are still coming through.

I started crying on the bathroom floor at 2am for a different reason. Two years of thinking Henry was a "hard case." Two years of believing I wasn't trying hard enough. None of it was true.

But the next thing I read made me angrier.

Because the article said you CAN rebuild the wall. With collagen. But not the kind of collagen most dog supplements use.

Most dog skin supplements use bovine collagen. Cow collagen. The molecules are over 20,000 Daltons. Way too big for a dog's gut to break down. So you pour it on his food, it goes through his stomach, and it comes out the other end without ever reaching the skin barrier.

You're paying $40, $60, sometimes $80 a bottle for something that physically cannot reach the place it's supposed to fix.

I sell some of these supplements in my grooming salon. I called my distributor on Monday morning and asked them to stop sending three of them.

The only collagen small enough to actually absorb into a dog's skin is marine collagen. From deep sea fish. The peptides are about one tenth the size of bovine. They get through the gut wall. They reach the bloodstream. They reach the skin barrier where the damage actually is.

And it's also 90% Type I, which is the exact type that builds skin and coat. Bovine collagen is mostly Type II, which is for joints. Most dog supplements are giving your dog joint collagen and calling it skin support.

The size is wrong AND the type is wrong.

So I went looking for one that matched the science. And I almost gave up before I found it.

Most products were the bovine kind. The big molecule kind. The kind that wouldn't work.

I finally found one. Marine collagen from deep sea fish. Hydrolyzed peptides under 3,000 Daltons. Dermatologist formulated. Liquid drops on his food once a day. Twenty dollars a bottle. About a dollar a day.

I almost didn't order it. I'd been burned too many times. But I'd just paid $189 for another Cytopoint shot that was going to fail in three weeks. Twenty dollars felt like nothing in comparison.

I clicked buy.

Three weeks later I was crying for a different reason.

The hot spot on his belly that had been there for two months started actually closing. Pink healthy skin where there had been gray.

A week after that he slept through the night without scratching. First time in over a year. I lay in bed listening to nothing and cried because I'd forgotten what nothing sounded like.

A week after that I took the cone off. The fur on the back of his neck started growing back.

A week after that I stopped the Apoquel. I held the four remaining pills in my hand for a long time. Then I put them in the trash. Held my breath for a week.

The itching never came back.

Twelve weeks in I took him for his annual. Different vet this time. She looked at his chart showing no medications in over a month and said "I don't understand. His skin looks healthier than the last time he was here."

I told her about the barrier. About marine collagen. About the size of the molecule.

She read the article on her phone right there in the exam room. "We don't really learn this in vet school. I had no idea the barrier was a factor."

She wasn't defensive. She was curious.

It's been six months. No Apoquel. No Cytopoint. No prescription food. No $400 months. Just one liquid on his food once a day. About a dollar.

Henry runs at the dog park now. His belly is smooth. His coat came back thick and shiny.

If you're where I was, please read what I read. It explains why every medication fails. Why the size of the collagen matters more than the dose. Why your dog might be stuck not because he's a hard case but because the wall is still broken.

It's not a sales page. It's the science that changed everything for me.

Your vet isn't wrong. They just weren't taught this.

But now you know.

— Lauren

title: Get Rid of Bacteria & Pet Odor from Your Washer

title: Feel Like Yourself Again
body_text:
I'm a nurse and I've been administering statins for 19 years, but last month I refused to take one myself.

I want to explain why. Because there's a sentence I've been legally unable to say in my professional capacity for almost two decades. And until three months ago, I kept my mouth shut.

I'm not keeping it shut anymore.

My name is Laura. I work nights in the ICU at a hospital I'm not going to name. 19 years on the same floor. I've held the hand of more dying people than I can count. Most of them were on a statin. Most of them had "perfectly controlled" cholesterol numbers in their chart.

That's the part that broke me eventually. I just didn't know it yet.

Here's what my job looks like. A patient gets admitted with chest pain or a full cardiac event. I pull up their chart. LDL 92. Total cholesterol 178. They've been on Lipitor or Crestor or Atorvastatin for eight, ten, twelve years. Their numbers look textbook.

And they're laying in front of me having a heart attack anyway.

The first few times it happens you tell yourself it's bad luck. Or genetics. Or the patient cheated on their diet. By year five you stop telling yourself stories. By year ten you start counting.

I started counting in 2019. I keep a number in my head now. I'm not going to share it because it would sound like I'm making it up. Just trust me when I say it's a lot of people. A lot of grandparents. A lot of fathers. A lot of men and women in their fifties, sixties, seventies, all who thought they were doing everything right.

All of them on a statin. All of them with "controlled" numbers. All of them dying anyway.

And I never said anything.

I want to be honest about that. Because you might be reading this thinking I'm some kind of whistleblower hero. I'm not. I'm a nurse who took an oath, who has a license to protect, who has a mortgage to pay, and who has been told for 19 years that if I question a doctor's prescription out loud in front of a patient I will lose all three.

That's not a metaphor. That's a real rule.

When a doctor writes a script for a statin, my job is to hand it to the patient and explain how to take it. If the patient asks me "do you think this will help?" I'm allowed to say "your doctor knows best." I'm not allowed to say what I actually think. I'm not allowed to mention what I've seen. I'm not allowed to tell them about the chart from last Tuesday where the same drug they're about to start was already failing somebody else.

If I do, I'm out of a job. Possibly out of a career.

So I learned to nod. To smile. To explain the dosing schedule. To go home and try to forget. And then I'd come back the next shift and do it again.

That was the deal I made for 19 years.

Three months ago the deal blew up.

I had my annual physical. Routine bloodwork. I'm 54, I exercise four days a week, I cook most of my own food, I haven't been overweight a day in my adult life. I wasn't worried about the labs.

The results came back and my LDL was 168.

I read the number twice. Then I read it again. Then I sat in my car in the parking lot for almost an hour because I knew exactly what was coming next.

Two days later my primary care doctor called me. "Laura, your numbers are concerning. I'd like to start you on a low dose Atorvastatin. We can talk about it at your follow-up but I'm sending the prescription to your pharmacy today."

He didn't ask. He told.

19 years of nodding and smiling collapsed in about four seconds. I drove home from work that night and I sat at my kitchen table and I cried. Not because I was scared of high cholesterol. Because I knew I was about to walk into the same machine I'd been feeding patients into for almost two decades.

And that machine doesn't work. I have spent 19 years watching it not work.

I let the prescription sit at the pharmacy. I didn't pick it up. I told my husband I needed a week to think about it. He's a paramedic. He's seen the same things I've seen. He didn't argue.

That week is when everything changed for me.

I started doing what I'd never let myself do as a working nurse. I started actually reading. Not the drug company pamphlets. Not the guidelines. The original studies. The stuff buried in the back of medical journals. The research nobody hands you on the floor because it complicates the story you're being paid to tell.

And I learned something that I now cannot believe I didn't know.

The number on your lipid panel was never the thing that was going to kill you.

I want to say that again because it took me a week to actually accept it. The number on your lipid panel was never the thing that was going to kill you. It was never the thing killing my patients either.

Here's what's actually happening.

Your liver makes cholesterol every day. It's supposed to. Cholesterol is not the enemy. Your brain needs it. Your cell membranes need it. Your hormones need it. Your liver puts cholesterol into your bloodstream and sends it out on a delivery route, dropping off what your cells need.

But your bloodstream is not a clean place. It's full of unstable molecules called free radicals. They come from stress, from processed food, from pollution, from sugar, from years of inflammation, from just getting older. And those free radicals attack the cholesterol while it's traveling.

They damage it.

Damaged cholesterol is a different substance entirely. It doesn't finish the route. It doesn't drop off. It sticks to the inside of your artery walls. And once it sticks, it stays there. More damaged cholesterol comes along and sticks right next to it. Layer on layer. That buildup is plaque. Plaque is what becomes the blockage. The blockage is what becomes the heart attack.

Not regular cholesterol. Damaged cholesterol.

And here is the part that broke my brain when I read it.

Your body doesn't know the cholesterol is stuck. It just knows it sent some out and it never came back. So it does what any well-designed system does when a delivery doesn't return. It makes more. It keeps producing replacement cholesterol to make up for what it's losing to the artery walls.

More gets damaged. More gets stuck. More gets replaced.

A cycle that feeds itself. The longer it runs, the higher the number on your panel climbs.

That's why your number won't come down.

Now I'm going to tell you what statins actually do, because I had to sit with this myself before I could believe it.

A statin forces your liver to stop producing cholesterol. That's the whole mechanism. It cuts off the manufacturing line. The number on your chart drops. Your doctor says great. Insurance is happy. The chart looks beautiful.

But the cholesterol that's already in your bloodstream? Still getting damaged. Still sticking. Still building up on your artery walls. The drug never touches the damage. It just lowers the supply.

Lowering the supply doesn't fix the cycle. It just hides it.

That's why my patients kept showing up in hospital with perfect numbers and failing hearts. The statin did exactly what it was advertised to do. It lowered the number. The number was never the problem.

The damage was the problem. And no statin has ever addressed it.

And it gets worse. Because the same biochemical pathway your liver uses to make cholesterol is the same one your body uses to make CoQ10. CoQ10 is the molecule your heart needs to beat 100,000 times a day. Your muscles need it to contract. Your brain needs it to think.

When a statin shuts down that pathway in your liver, it shuts down CoQ10 production too. Your heart loses its primary energy source. Your muscles lose their fuel. That's the muscle pain people on statins describe. That's the brain fog. That's the bone-deep exhaustion patients tell me about. That's the "feeling like I aged 20 years overnight."

That's not aging. That's the drug.

I have charted those complaints for 19 years. I have watched doctor after doctor write "common side effect, benefits outweigh risks" and move on. I have watched patients be told their muscle pain was "in their head." That the brain fog was "just normal aging." That they were imagining it.

They weren't imagining it. They were being slowly drained of the molecule their heart needs to keep beating. By the drug that was supposed to be protecting their heart.

After 19 years of watching it, I have an opinion. I'll keep it professional. But I have one.

That week at my kitchen table, I went looking for the alternative. I'd seen the rest of the menu fail too. Oatmeal works in your gut, grabbing some cholesterol before it enters your blood. Fine, but it can't protect cholesterol that's already circulating. Fish oil nudges triglycerides down. Doesn't stop the damage. Garlic, niacin, plant sterols, red yeast rice, bergamot, berberine. I've watched patients try every one of them.

Every single one works downstream. None of them stop the damage that's making the cholesterol stick in the first place.

I was about to give up and pick up the prescription when I found a study from the Indian Council of Medical Research. Then another from the Journal of Ethnopharmacology. Then a 2020 review pulling them all together.

They were all about a superfruit called Amla. Gooseberry.

I'd never heard of it. Most American clinicians haven't. It's not on the cardiology board exam. It's not in the medical guidelines. It barely shows up on the supplement aisle at Walgreens.

But Himalayan healers have been using it for over five thousand years. They called it "the nurse." It was the remedy they reached for when somebody's body was breaking down from the inside.

And modern science finally figured out why it worked.

Amla contains specific compounds called emblicanins. They're a class of antioxidant found almost nowhere else in nature. When researchers tested the antioxidant strength of over a thousand foods, Amla ranked at the top. Higher than blueberries. Higher than green tea. Higher than turmeric. And it wasn't even close.

Here's what emblicanins do.

They go into your bloodstream and they neutralize the free radicals before those free radicals can damage your cholesterol. Not in the gut like oatmeal. Not on triglycerides like fish oil. In the bloodstream, where the actual damage happens.

When cholesterol is better protected from damage, less of it ends up sticking to your artery walls.

When less is sticking, your body has less reason to keep over producing to replace what it's losing.

The cycle starts to ease up.

Your number can start coming down. Not because something forced your liver to shut down the way a statin does. Because your body doesn't need to keep over producing to replace what's being lost.

Then I found the study that made me close my laptop and sit there for ten minutes staring at the wall.

In a 12-week clinical trial, standardized Amla extract was tested alongside a low-dose statin. The Amla performed comparably. LDL came down significantly. Triglycerides came down. HDL improved. And the participants didn't see the CoQ10 depletion, the muscle pain, or the brain fog that I've been documenting in my charts for 19 years.

A superfruit extract. Going head to head with the prescription that was sitting in my pharmacy. And matching it.

I sat at my kitchen table thinking about every patient I'd held the hand of in the ICU. Every grandfather. Every mother of three. Every grandmother who had eight, ten, twelve years of "well controlled" numbers and a heart attack anyway.

The thing that could have actually supported them at the level the damage was happening has existed the entire time. And nobody told them.

Nobody.

That was the moment I stopped being a quiet nurse.

I did what nurses do before we trust something. I checked the product. Because not all Amla is the same. Most of what you'll find online is cheap fruit powder with degraded compounds and no third party testing. Some is contaminated with heavy metals from poor sourcing. Some uses fillers. Some is heat processed, which destroys the emblicanins that make it work in the first place.

The difference between raw Amla powder and a properly standardized extract is the difference between chewing willow bark and taking an aspirin. One is the plant. The other is the concentrated, verified compound that actually produces the result.

I went with Alevia's Amla. Organic. Third party tested. Made in the USA. Small batch production to preserve the active compounds. No fillers. No heat processing. The kind of standardization the clinical trials used.

Two capsules every morning. With water. Before my shift.

I never picked the Atorvastatin up from the pharmacy.

I want to be honest about what the first few days felt like. It wasn't anything.

No buzz. No surge. Amla isn't caffeine. It doesn't announce itself. It works in your bloodstream where the damage actually happens, and that takes time to show up anywhere you can measure.

So I just took my two capsules with water before my shift. Drove to work. Did my rounds. Came home. Took them again the next morning.

Then the small things started.

End of week one. I drove home from a 12 hour overnight on a Saturday morning and I didn't fall asleep at a red light on the way. I'd been micro-sleeping at red lights on the drive home for the better part of a decade. That morning I just drove home awake.

Week two. My husband looked at me over his coffee and said "your face looks different. Less puffy. Like you slept better than you actually slept." I hadn't slept better. I hadn't changed anything except the two capsules.

That's the first phase. The emblicanins start neutralizing the free radicals attacking your cholesterol. The oxidative stress eases. You don't feel the chemistry. You feel the noise lifting.

Week three. I went up the hospital stairs two at a time the way I always have, got to the top, and wasn't out of breath. I'd been telling myself the breathlessness on the stairs was "just being 54." It wasn't.

Week four. I started waking up before my alarm without that lead-in-the-arms feeling nurses know. The bone heavy tired that never fully leaves. It was just gone.

That's the second phase. Less cholesterol getting damaged. Less sticking. Your body easing off the replacement production. The cycle starts to break.

Week six I bought a finger prick lipid test at my own pharmacy. Sat at the kitchen table with my husband. Pricked my finger.

LDL: 142. Down from 168.

26 points in six weeks. And I never picked up the prescription.

I sat there holding the strip and I started crying. Not because of the number. Because of every patient. Every chart with "controlled" numbers and a heart attack anyway. The thing that would have actually helped them was a fruit extract. And nobody had told them.

That's the third phase. The full panel starts moving. LDL down. HDL up. Triglycerides down. Numbers you can finally look at.

I had my actual lipid panel at week 11.

LDL: 124. Down 44 points. HDL up. Triglycerides down.

My primary care doctor called the next morning. "Laura, did you start the Atorvastatin?"

"No."

Four seconds of silence. I've been a nurse long enough to know what that silence means. A doctor recalibrating in real time.

"What did you do?"

I told him. The studies on oxidation. Emblicanins. The clinical trial against Simvastatin. The fact that the number was never the actual problem. I talked for 15 minutes. He didn't interrupt once.

He was quiet for a long time. Then he said "I don't know much about Amla. But your numbers have come down significantly. Let's keep monitoring and talk again at your next panel."

19 years of biting my tongue. And my own doctor just said the words I'd been waiting to hear my entire career.

I held it together until I got to my car. Then I sat in the parking lot and cried.

That's the fourth phase. Long term. The emblicanins keep working. The cycle stays broken. Your numbers don't just come down once. They stay where they're supposed to be. Without a single milligram of a drug that was going to drain CoQ10 out of every muscle in your body.

I cried because I was off the hook. I cried because every patient I'd held the hand of in the ICU should have been off the hook too. I cried because the answer was a fruit. And nobody had told them.

That's why I'm writing this.

I'm writing this because I cannot keep doing this anymore.

I cannot keep nodding and smiling and handing out prescriptions to people whose only "crime" was trusting their doctor to give them the full picture. I cannot keep watching ICU admissions on patients with "controlled" numbers and saying nothing.

If you have high cholesterol and your doctor is reaching for the prescription pad, I want you to read this twice. Your number is not the thing that's going to hurt you. The damage to the cholesterol is the thing that's going to hurt you. And there is no statin on the market that addresses the damage. They lower the number. The cycle keeps running underneath.

If you're already on a statin and you're feeling the muscle pain, the brain fog, the exhaustion that wasn't there before, you're not imagining it. You're not aging at warp speed. The drug is doing exactly what it's designed to do, and what it's designed to do has costs your doctor has been told to call "manageable."

If you've tried oatmeal, fish oil, garlic, red yeast rice, bergamot, niacin, the whole supplement aisle, and your number isn't moving, that's because none of them stop the damage. They were never built to.
